Now what?', give concrete recognition shapes (exact-target-sum reconciliation, order-dependent-cost routing, conflict-free assignment, budgeted best-value subset) and a ranked set of real responses (exact solve when the instance is small/bounded, PTAS/FPTAS when a bounded gap is acceptable, heuristics with a cheap-relaxation bound otherwise) — none of that appears on the Wikipedia page for the same query, which I fetched directly and confirmed has no such section and zero runnable code anywhere. Structure is intentionally question-driven (nearly every H2 is a question, e.g. 'What does "NP" mean — checking, not solving?'), which is a real, deliberate choice distinct from sibling complexity-pillar articles: I checked big-o-notation.md and amortized-analysis.md and both use declarative statement headings throughout, with no direct heading overlap or reused phrasing against this article. Front matter is accurate and non-clickbait: title and description both state precisely what the piece does, and the description is 159 characters — inside the required 110-160 range (I counted it directly; the writer's note about trimming from 165 checks out). Copying/close-paraphrase check: every quoted fragment attributed to a NIST DADS page or the Clay Institute is a verbatim match — I fetched all 14 cited DADS pages plus the Clay page directly and checked each quotation string by string, including the one that looked riskiest on first read, the NP-complete 'informal' quote ('answers can be verified quickly, and a quick algorithm to solve this problem can be used to solve all other NP problems quickly'): that exact sentence is genuinely present on NIST's own npcomplete.html page as its informal gloss, not a fabrication or an altered quote. Paraphrased (non-quoted) material — the polynomial-time restatement, the PTAS/FPTAS descriptions, the knapsack NP-completeness mention — is expressed in the article's own words and structure, not lifted phrasing, and the worked examples (invoice reconciliation, the print-job-flavored recognition list, the buggy index-based verifier) are original, not reused from any cited source. `run-code.mjs` passes clean (blocks=17, executed=7). run-code.mjs passes clean. Two things keep this below the pass bar. First (major): the article has two measured-timing sections that print real wall-clock numbers ('One run on this machine printed:', the brute-force growth table and the DP-scaling table) but never states, anywhere in the piece, what machine or toolchain produced them — I grepped the full body for 'Windows', '.NET <version>', 'x64' and CPU-class words and found none. EDITORIAL_BRIEF.md's binding pilot-round lessons require stating the toolchain once, in the writer's own words, at the point measurements appear, specifically so a reader can judge whether 'roughly quadruples every two items' or 'doubles with the target' is a property of the algorithm or an artifact of one unknown machine; this article has real measured numbers with the disclosure the brief requires them to carry, missing. Second (minor): the sentence 'The first NP-complete problem, Boolean satisfiability (SAT), was identified this way by Stephen Cook and, independently, Leonid Levin, both in 1971' states a discovery year for Levin that doesn't match the standard account — Cook's paper was published in 1971, but Levin's independent result was published in 1973 (Wikipedia's Cook–Levin theorem page, fetched directly, dates it that way, noting only that it had circulated in talks/submissions 'a few years earlier'). The underlying claim (Cook and Levin, independently) is correct and this is a small date compression rather than a fabrication, but it is a checkable factual claim stated as settled fact and it is not quite right as written.

issues.problem: States 1971 as Levin's discovery year alongside Cook's. Cook's paper was published in 1971; Levin's independent result was published in 1973 (Wikipedia's Cook–Levin theorem article, fetched directly, gives 1973 for Levin's publication, noting only that it had been mentioned in talks/submitted a few years earlier than that). 'Both in 1971' compresses a commonly-cited two-year gap into one date for a claim presented as settled historical fact.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either give both years separately ('Cook, in 1971, and independently Leonid Levin, whose paper appeared in 1973') or soften to 'in the early 1970s' if a single approximate date is preferred, with a citation for the Cook/Levin history if one isn't already in the sources list.
